title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
abstract: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.

title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.

title: Multi-site Learning for Forecasting Day-Ahead Wind-Power Production for Onshore Wind Farms in Great Britain with Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Accurate day-ahead wind-power production forecasting is increasingly important for energy system operations, market activity and balancing Great Britain's grid as wind generation grows. In this study, we train multi-site deep neural networks (DNNs) using pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind Balancing Mechanism Units (BMUs). Forecasts are produced at 09:00 UK time for the following midnight-to-midnight delivery day, matching NESO's operational day-ahead forecasting schedule. We use reanalysis weather as future covariates during training and numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts during inference, extending training beyond the available historical NWP archive. Our multi-site recurrent neural network outperforms site-specific RNNs and a multi-site XGBoost model, while processing the full future-weather trajectory for the forecast horizon further improves accuracy relative to hour-aligned approaches. Our best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (BiRNN) for NWP trajectory processing, reduces MW mean absolute error and root mean squared error relative to NESO by 17.94% and 12.51%, respectively, across 638,246 matched BMU-hour observations under conditions approximating unconstrained wind farm operations. In 40 leave-one-out trials, the BiRNN achieves lower MAE than NESO at 32 excluded sites, indicating transferable forecasting ability despite reduced accuracy when sites are omitted from training. Our capacity-estimation, data-cleaning and reanalysis-based training approach provides a basis for scaling NWP-aware multi-site forecasting to additional wind farms, longer production histories, and increased forecast accuracy beyond that seen in this study.

title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
abstract: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.

title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.

title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.

title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.

title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.

title: Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data
abstract: Class-conditional conformal prediction calibrates a separate score threshold for every class and therefore requires labelled calibration examples of every class. In long-tailed deployments these are exactly what is missing: rare classes are left with few or no held-out examples, and existing methods are either undefined for them or fall back to the shared marginal threshold. We ask whether the per-class correction can instead be predicted from descriptors of the class that require no labels at all. We propose Predicted Class Correction (PCC), which regresses the offset between the per-class and the marginal conformal quantile on geometric descriptors of the classifier head, shrinks the prediction by a scalar selected on the labelled classes, and refits a single marginal offset. The descriptors depend only on the model's weights, so a class with zero calibration examples still receives its own threshold, and since only one scalar is calibrated, split conformal's marginal guarantee is retained. On ImageNet, PCC improves worst-class coverage on such classes by 0.058 [0.006, 0.110] at matched average set size, 42% of an oracle that sees the test labels. Of eight baselines on the same splits, six change the statistic by exactly zero and the best reaches 0.016 with an interval containing zero, so PCC is the only one distinguishable from no improvement; the gain persists with only 100 labelled classes out of 1000. A second finding concerns evaluation: worst-class coverage becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable. Below roughly 35 test examples per class no improvement can be shown even for an oracle, so a null result there reflects the evaluation set, not the method. Restricting evaluation above this depth recovers a significant improvement on Pl@ntNet-300K, where the effect had appeared absent.

title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.

title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
abstract:
The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting.
  We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.

title: Follow the Mixed Groups: Ridge-Tracking Gaussian Sampling for Zero-Variance Web Rollouts
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a question only when the sampled responses disagree. A group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has zero reward variance and a zero advantage. On the Web, that group has already spent its searches and page fetches. Gaussian curricula aim the next batch at pass rates where a finite group can still mix. A Gaussian on the latest empirical rate treats every all-fail history as the same point, and a center stepped by the average signed change of those rates is pushed by prompts already stuck at 0 or 1. RIDGE keeps the Gaussian curriculum and changes the coordinate, the center, and the width. Each prompt carries a Beta posterior. The sampling weight is the marginal of a Gaussian target under a Gaussian approximation of that posterior, divided by a prediction of tool-call cost. The center and the width are an exponential smooth of the posterior means of groups that just came back mixed. All-correct and all-incorrect groups refresh the posterior and do not move the center. The GRPO update itself is unchanged. On two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, RIDGE raises average accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points over GRPO and average exact match by 3.7 points, at 29.6\% fewer math rollouts and 32.7\% fewer tool calls than dynamic sampling.
relevance_reason: 该论文提出RIDGE，一种改进GRPO课程采样的方法，通过Beta后验和Gaussian近似来优化rollout效率。这是纯粹的RL训练/在线策略优化方法，用于提升Web搜索增强推理训练效率。没有任何量化、剪枝、蒸馏、KV cache压缩等模型压缩内容。完全属于RL训练优化范畴，触发hard_gate。

title: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a prompt only when the rewards in the sampled group disagree. With a binary verifier, a group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has within-group variance zero and a zero advantage. Uniform sampling continues to spend rollouts on prompts that are unanimous now and stay unanimous as training goes on. Pass rate is a weak forecast of that future. Two prompts at the same pass rate can move apart: one into the range where a finite group splits, and one toward a ceiling where the group becomes unanimous again. Aperture estimates the later pass rate from a short probe. A small subset of the pool is trained with the same recipe, every prompt is scored on the base model and on the probe model, and the two pass rates are plugged into the probability that a group of the training size is all wrong or split. The resulting weight is a static prior. It can be used alone or multiplied by an online scheduler, and the GRPO update is left as it is. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, the prior improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and raises the fraction of groups with a nonzero advantage. The same prior still helps when it is combined with dynamic sampling or with selective rollouts.
relevance_reason: 本文提出Aperture，一种用于GRPO（Group Relative Policy Optimization）训练的静态采样先验，通过估计每个prompt的未来组内方差来优化rollout采样效率。这是纯粹的RL后训练（post-training）优化方法，不涉及任何量化、剪枝、蒸馏、KV cache压缩或其他模型压缩技术。主要贡献是改进GRPO的课程/采样策略，与LLM compression完全无关，属于alignment/RL训练方法，hard_gate=true。

title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.

title: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
abstract: Deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory permits local post-hoc knowledge injection. Extending arXiv:2610.21553's bounded-feasibility audit rejecting under-specified generality claims with repaired probes and training-dose/capacity axes, we give, to our knowledge, the first production-scale write-content verdict. We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.

title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.
relevance_reason: 本文研究Transformer在图路径规划中的错误检测机制，通过训练模型识别无效转移并生成abort token来提升规划可靠性。这是一项纯粹的机制研究（mechanistic study），既无量化压缩、剪枝、蒸馏，也无KV cache压缩，与LLM压缩/推理优化完全无关。评估基准是图路径规划、Countdown和迷宫任务，不属于任何标准LLM压缩基准。不符合八个压缩bucket中的任何一个，应hard_gate。

title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.

title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

title: The Explainability Illusion: Must ViTs Exhibit Patch-Decoding Interpretability?
abstract: Transformers are widely assumed to exhibit token-decoding explainability. In particular, in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers, decoding individual patch tokens has become a common diagnostic tool due to its tendency to yield human-interpretable outputs. In light of the increasing popularity of this approach, an important question is whether token-decoding explainability is an inherent property of transformers that should be expected to hold across architectures, scales, and training objectives, or merely an artifact of some implicit bias. In this paper we systematically study token-decoding explainability across diverse ViT settings, spanning architectures, scales, and training objectives, using both controlled experiments and real-world models. We find that while some models indeed exhibit aligned and interpretable token decodings, others exhibit either inverted explainability maps or a complete lack of correlation with the image semantics. As we show, these tendencies toward different explainability behaviors are not intrinsic to the architecture and can vary arbitrarily with changes in the optimization landscape. We provide theoretical support for these observations by demonstrating a setting where a single fixed toy transformer architecture can provably implement the optimal classification rule in multiple ways, which differ in their patch-decoding explainability patterns. Our results show that token-decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers, but rather an outcome contingent on the problem setting and thus should not be a-priori assumed to hold. Code can be found in https://ronensc.github.io/Explainability-Illusion/ .

title: A discrete-continuous-time stochastic framework for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptom modeling and pharmacological intervention via methylphenidate
abstract: This paper presents an original mathematical and computational framework for modeling the efficacy of methylphenidate as an optimal control policy acting on the nonlinear dynamics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Neural processes in ADHD are conceptualized as stochastic processes with trajectories that inherently converge towards stable, yet dysfunctional patterns associated with clinical symptoms. The pharmacological intervention is mathematically formalized as an external control signal that reassesses the system's drift and redirects these trajectories towards neurotypical regimes. To bridge these theoretical stochastic models with empirical clinical data, latent representations are inferred using a novel deterministic hybrid deep learning architecture, combining a one-dimensional convolutional neural network and a Vision Transformer, trained on preprocessed functional magnetic resonance imaging data.

title: Data-driven forecasting of tropical cloud forest phenology: A dynamical systems and machine learning hybrid approach
abstract:
Forecasting how species and ecosystems respond to climate change is a critical challenge in ecology, particularly in hyper-diverse tropical biomes. While traditional phenological models often rely on preconceived functional forms, this study introduces a data-driven hybrid approach that integrates dynamical systems theory with machine learning to forecast flowering and fruiting cycles.
  Using a robust 35-year dataset from a Venezuelan tropical cloud forest, we reconstruct the system's state-space using delay vectors inspired by Takens' theorem, incorporating climate forcing variables such as temperature and precipitation. The model was trained using Gaussian Process Regression, providing both point predictors and explicit uncertainty estimates.
  Our results clearly suggest that the synergy between dynamical systems and machine learning effectively captures the non-linear complexities of ecological time series. Specifically, the model achieved higher predictive accuracy for flowering and fruiting. This hybrid framework offers a scalable tool for anticipating phenological mismatches and informing conservation strategies in the face of global environmental change.

title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. To this end, we introduce new benchmark datasets constructed from CIKM, KDD, and SIGIR conference papers, with varied prediction settings, including impact forecasting for emerging concepts unseen during training. We propose MiroGraph, a Multi-agent reasoning framework with scientific concept Graphs, in which a feature designer agent designs predictive features for a given concept pair from structural, semantic, and trend perspectives, and then three LLM agents compute the actual feature values from the enclosing subgraph of the concept pair. Using these feature values, a classifier designer agent constructs a classifier that predicts the final impact labels. MiroGraph outperforms various impact forecasting and temporal link prediction methods.

title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
abstract: LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (EG-GRPO), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.

title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
abstract: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.

title: Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity
abstract: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.

title: EasyResearch: Honest Regression, Forecasting and Signal Classification for Researchers Who Do Not Program
abstract: EasyClassifier showed that researchers who do not program can obtain honest classification results when the correct evaluation is the default. Most applied studies, however, predict a number, forecast a series or classify recordings, and each task has its own way of producing scores that do not hold on new data. We present EasyResearch, open-source analysis cores for regression, time-series forecasting and signal classification, and EasyResearch Desktop, a Windows application that runs these three tasks and EasyClassifier's classification without code. All four follow the same rules: everything learned from data is learned on training data only, models keep their published defaults with fixed seeds, the selected model receives a separate final score, forecasts are never evaluated on shuffled data, and every run writes a report with a Methods paragraph and the references for every method used. We measured whether the reported scores are honest by keeping part of each dataset untouched. In regression (9 public datasets, 90 runs), the common practice overstated R^2 by +2.2 points and the best comparison score by +2.5, while EasyResearch's final score was -1.0; screening predictors on all rows before cross-validation, which EasyResearch does not offer, reported R^2 = 0.27 on pure noise against -0.44 on new data. In forecasting (15 series), shuffled cross-validation over windows of past values promised errors 19% smaller than its chosen models achieved in the untouched future, while EasyResearch's final-period score was unbiased to within 1.5%; the models EasyResearch chose had 14% lower future error, and on random walks shuffled cross-validation chose a machine-learning model in 5 of 5 series, each worse in the future than repeating the last value, which EasyResearch chose 4 times. In signal classification (4 UCR datasets) one method won every comparison and neither estimate was biased.

title: Emergent Sparsity: How Many Effective Variables Survive Coarse-Graining in AlphaEarth Embeddings?
abstract: AlphaEarth encodes each 10 m land pixel as a 64-component vector intended to support diverse global mapping tasks. Yet many scientific applications work at coarser spatial supports, for which fewer than 64 effective variables may suffice. We ask whether these vectors can be reorganized into ranked global nonlinear coordinates, how many suffice at a chosen reconstruction accuracy, and whether that number decreases with spatial scale. We thus describe effective dimension as a two-control surface over tolerance and spatial scale, rather than one intrinsic number. At each scale, a $β$-VAE scan with a common architecture produces a rank--distortion envelope, giving the smallest retained count achieved within the scanned family at each reconstruction tolerance. At 3% validation tolerance, this number falls from 24 to 7 when the scale is increased from 10 m to 78.9 km, whereas the corresponding PCA rank falls only from 46 to 38. Repeating the analysis on unit-norm targets preserves this trend.

title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models
abstract: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.

title: Persistent Representational Misalignment Induces Vision-Language Model Failures
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-$κ$ KV-cache access require $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size $n$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the \emph{Multi-hop Retrieval Attention} (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size $m$-hop MuRA block can compute $m$-function composition, whereas computing $(m+1)$-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.

title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
abstract: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.

title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

title: DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices
abstract: Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.

title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20--30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10--15%.

title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
abstract: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[\mathbb{Z}_\ell]$, which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as $[[169,13,11]]$, $[[143,15,9]]$, and $[[260,24,10]]$, including a $[[247,19,14]]$ code that achieves the highest ${kd^2}/{n}$ among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.

title: Calibration-Free Early Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via E-processes
abstract: Reasoning large language models (LLMs) benefit from test-time scaling, motivating adaptive policies that spend tokens when they help and stop early otherwise. Existing rules halt when a confidence or stability signal crosses a threshold, but such thresholds rarely transfer across models and datasets, and validation-calibrated rules lose their guarantee under shifts in test-time horizon or signal dynamics. We reframe adaptive stopping as sequential evidence accumulation along the reasoning trajectory rather than threshold calibration on held-out data. Our framework runs two e-processes on a shared per-chunk signal: a commit stream tracks the signal's position relative to its slow trend, and an abstain stream tracks its signed velocity, making the two anti-correlated by construction. Under signal-level nulls on the per-chunk increments, Ville's inequality yields an anytime-valid signal-level false-alarm bound at user-specified significance levels, with no held-out calibration. Across various model--dataset combinations, the framework matches or exceeds calibration-based stopping on the token--accuracy Pareto front using zero calibration data, and the same significance level transfers unchanged across cells where calibration becomes infeasible.

title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research
abstract: EEG analysis and decoding underpin brain-computer interfaces, cognitive assessment, and sleep monitoring. Fixed pipelines and reward-driven search do not explicitly determine how signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics contribute to performance or generalization gaps, leaving intervention choice underdetermined. We introduce NeuroAct, an autonomous research agent framework for EEG analysis and decoding. NeuroAct implements dual-loop autonomous research across EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and model combinations. In an inner loop, research, development, and review roles use evidence on signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics to test hypotheses, select analyses or interventions, and refine candidates using performance, stability, and cost feedback. An outer loop distills outcomes into conditional, testable recommendations with task and model conditions, then validates and revises them on subsequent tasks.We evaluate four settings: (A) EEG General Analysis, (B) Cross-task Model Optimization, (C) Single-task Open Research, and (D) Collaborative Prediction. In Setting A, NeuroAct's 80.88 macro-average exceeds BrainAgent's 63.13 by 17.75 points. In Setting B, NeuroAct raises EEGPT's mean balanced accuracy (BA) by 7.34 points and HBN Pearson's (r) from 0.6894 to 0.7362; in Setting C, it improves ADFTD BA by 16.33 points; and in Setting D, it raises Workload BA from 79.69% to 85.02%. Experience reuse raises BCIC-IV-2a BA from 34.66% to 50.81% while reducing LLM tokens by 64.02%, indicating recommendations improve cross-task performance. NeuroAct enables evidence-guided EEG research improved by cross-task experience.

title: A Thousand Faces: A Persuasion Benchmark with Experience-Grounded Persuadees Informed by Psychology and Pragmatics
abstract: People can express the same beliefs and desires yet need different reasons to change their minds. What makes an argument relevant depends on how those views arose: experiences shape what a person finds credible, what matters to them, and what could prompt reconsideration. These personal grounds may also be expressed indirectly, through contextual clues in conversation. Benchmarks that specify beliefs and desires without these connections can reward arguments that match a description while overlooking whether they address the person's reasons. We introduce A Thousand Faces (ATF-Persu), with 1,000 personas across 200 topics and nine domains. Drawing on personality and attitude theories and conversational implicature, we construct five personas per factual context, linking experiences to judgments, expression, and grounds for revision. Evaluations show lower persuasion success than three comparison benchmarks under their respective protocols. Complete backgrounds yield broader use of supplied personal grounds and higher persona faithfulness than simplified specifications; blinded reviewers also rate ATF-Persu above CToMPersu on identifiable personal reasons, their influence on responses, and contextual expression. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Slandes/ATF-Persu.

title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image-text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut-solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual-residual-based data selection method for Med-VLM fine-tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image-dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity-aware fine-tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi-disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR-selected 20\% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full-data fine-tuning and selection baselines. Gradient-level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image-dependent training signals and strengthens image-level and evidence-region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/ViCoR.

title: RAIL-5G: A Challenging Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for AI-Based 5G Indoor Localization
abstract: Reliable radio-based indoor localization is essential for industrial automation, yet existing methods are often evaluated in environments that do not fully reflect the severe multipath and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions encountered in real deployments. This limits our understanding of how AI, i.e., modern geometric, unsupervised, and semi-supervised localization methods generalize to industrial 5G settings. We present RAIL-5G, a public real-world 5G NR channel impulse response (CIR) benchmark recorded in an operational railway maintenance facility. RAIL-5G covers an 811m$^2$ indoor area with eight distributed radio units, robot-mounted user equipment (UE) trajectories, high-accuracy iGPS reference positions, and severe metal-induced multipath caused by train compartments and maintenance infrastructure. We benchmark geometric time-difference of arrival (TDoA), supervised fingerprinting, unsupervised channel charting, and self-supervised wireless pretraining methods. Our results highlight the difficulty of RAIL-5G: on the full dataset, TDoA reaches 7.02m mean average error (MAE), the best unsupervised method reaches 2.46m, and supervised fingerprinting achieves 0.52m. Self-supervised pretraining reduces the labeling effort by up to one order of magnitude, but the remaining gap to supervised learning shows that robust AI-based localization under severe multipath remains an open challenge. The dataset and code are available at https://iis.fraunhofer.de/rail-5g.

title: ChronoChart: Setup-Agnostic Channel Charting for Label-Free Indoor Localization
abstract: Accurate radio-based indoor localization remains challenging in multipath-rich and dynamic indoor environments. Supervised fingerprinting methods achieve high positioning accuracy by learning mappings from radio channel measurements to physical locations, but require costly position labels and frequent recalibration. Channel Charting (CC) addresses this limitation by learning low-dimensional representations of Channel State Information (CSI) without position labels, yielding channel charts in which nearby points correspond to nearby physical locations. However, prominent CC methods rely on setup-specific dissimilarity metrics, such as ADP-, CIRA-, or PDR-based distances, and on precomputed $O(n^2)$ distance matrices, limiting scalability and transferability across radio systems. We propose ChronoChart, a timestamp-supervised CC framework that requires only CSI and timestamps without prior knowledge for training. Our method jointly optimizes complementary objectives: a triplet loss using temporally derived positive and negative samples to establish coarse global structure, a temporal-proximity loss that promotes smooth trajectories in the chart, and a joint-embedding loss that enforces consistency between representations of different augmentations. Evaluated on real-world 5G, MIMO, and passive UWB data, our method matches or exceeds prior CC baselines that depend on tailored distance metrics, and remains scalable and applicable across heterogeneous radio systems.

title: Shallow Probes Are Sufficient for Near-Oracle Personalization Depth Allocation in Federated Learning
abstract: Rather than proposing a new federated optimizer, we study whether a small client-specific measurement budget can support cost-aware personalization-depth decisions under a utility that trades Macro-F1 against deployment cost. Exhaustive evaluation of six depths defines an offline oracle that is not deployable. We audit the Probe Sufficiency Hypothesis: three shallow probes (P0--P2) may contain most decision-relevant information for approaching that oracle. FedPBA is a secondary learned instantiation for deep-action extrapolation. On CIFAR-10/100 and patient-disjoint PTB-XL (45 sessions; 900 clients; 2700 evaluations; GroupKFold), training-free greedy probing achieves regret 0.0071 and 98.3 percent oracle recovery, beating metadata-only policies and FedPBA (0.0110 / 97.3 percent). Aggregate shallow-best versus oracle correlation is 0.9818 but falls to 0.578 on deep-oracle rows; PTB-XL deep-oracle cases remain a high-regret boundary without a validated escalation gate.

title: Acharya 2.0: An AI Tutor for Self-Learning Subjects in Hindi
abstract: Text processing is crucial for low-resource languages as it enables the development of tools and technologies that bridge the digital divide and provide equitable access to information and services. By empowering low-resource languages with robust text processing, we can preserve linguistic diversity, enhance education, improve communi- cation, and foster inclusivity in a rapidly digitizing world. Due to the lack of sufficient annotated datasets and lin- guistic resources, it is challenging to develop accurate and reliable language technologies for these low-resource languages. Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted sig- nificant attention with their performance and the value they produce. However, with the ever-evolving language, adapting LLMs for a specific task is time-consuming and resource-intensive. Thus, Retrieval-Augmented Genera- tion (RAG) has overcome this limitation by augmenting LLMs with external knowledge, thereby improving their efficiency and extensive task-specific adaptation. Most applications of the RAG technique have been limited to English and has seen limited application in In- dic languages. This paper introduces the RAG-powered AI-Tutor application, Acharya 2.0, designed to produce academic assistance to Hindi-speaking students. The client-server-based web application integrates many fea- tures to support students in accessing and interacting with educational content.

title: Sampling and Curvature in First-Exit Comparisons for Momentum SGD
abstract: First-exit prediction for momentum SGD depends on sampling information that pointwise gradient laws omit. Strongly convex finite pools with identical pointwise laws and matched iid momentum dynamics can have different reshuffled exits; even analytic pools with uniformly close pointwise laws can have separated exit probabilities. For persistent sampling in one dimension, we establish an explicit $O(h)$ mean-exit comparison with a finite-rate switching process under nonvanishing component velocities and step-size conditions; iid sampling instead averages to an ODE. Retaining realized minibatches and sampled curvature yields finite-window exit brackets beyond this regime. In 32 trained ridge-logistic runs, 29 meet prespecified targets with rounding-certified brackets; an enclosure control explains most of the width advantage. Exact-real certificates establish finite means at the original tested radii for three ResNet-18 checkpoints and give local finite-mean conditions for tanh and ViT networks; their upper bounds remain loose, and original-radius ViT mean guarantees remain unresolved despite 128 fresh continuation paths. A two-network replication gives 32/32 successful seeds in each of four finite-path persistence comparisons. Independent equal-length controls retain slower exits after refresh resets than without resets, but the refresh-versus-random ordering reverses with update length at both networks. These interventions do not causally decompose raw momentum SGD. Neural step-size scaling does not validate the switching limit.

title: Reranking Answers of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Answering natural language questions over knowledge graph data is challenging due to the vast number of facts, which can be difficult to process and navigate. One potential solution for this issue is to use mined subgraphs related to the query, although this process still requires extracting these subgraphs. This research presents a solution for extracting subgraphs related to entity candidates from a question-and-answer set, which can be obtained by inferring a large language model by calculating the shortest paths between entities. The proposed approaches detail various features that can be extracted from the subgraphs and reranking models to select the most probable answers from a list of candidates. Experiments were conducted on Wikidata to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. This involved enumerating all the main feature types that can be extracted from mined subgraphs and a detailed analysis of the proposed features and reranking method combinations. In addition, a public web application that provides a useful web tool for studying the graph space between question and answer entities has been developed to work with subgraphs. This includes visualization of the extracted subgraph and automatic generation of natural language text to describe it.

title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Toward an Interdisciplinary Study of Meaning Variation
abstract: An increasing number of disciplines recognize the explanatory potential of meaning-bearing mental structures through which individuals interpret the world and guide their behavior. Concept representations constitute a core class of these structures, emerging from individuals' experiences with concept referents and encoding and organizing their understanding of them. Recognizing a private level of meaning, where concepts are not objectively defined by rules in the world but constitute subjective structures in individuals' minds, raises a fundamental question: do different individuals actually mean the same thing when they invoke the same concept? As latent structures, concept representations are difficult to access and model empirically. The present study introduces a measurement framework that makes such representations empirically accessible through textual traces elicited under standardized conditions. Using transformer-based sentence embeddings, the framework maps standardized responses elicited for concepts into a high-dimensional shared vector space, opening concept representations to the systematic analysis of interindividual variation. It develops three analytical avenues: (1) comparing representational sharedness across concepts, (2) identifying variables that correlate with representational variation, and (3) examining how focal actors or subpopulations deviate from a reference population. Each avenue is illustrated through an empirical proof-of-concept drawing on a large-scale free-association dataset. Together, the demonstrations show how researchers from across disciplines can move from a research question and data source to analysis and interpretation. An accompanying GitHub repository provides a ready-to-use implementation of the framework for existing and custom datasets.

title: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents acting as the seeker and recommender generate utterances according to turn-level constraints. To support recommendation, the recommender is provided with knowledge graphs constructed from metadata about the content items used in each dialogue, capturing their attributes and relationships. Using SearCl, we generate 3,538 dialogues from content search and click interaction data, covering 1,731 unique target items. Under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, the resulting dialogues achieve higher quality scores than dialogues from existing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that SearCl enables controllable and knowledge-grounded dataset construction without human annotations.

title: Memory, Know Your PLACE: Governing Lifecycle State and Query-Time Eligibility in Persistent-Memory Agents
abstract: Persistent memory turns prior interactions into durable agent state, but existing systems provide limited control over whether that state remains valid and whether it should influence a later query. We argue that reliable memory requires governance over both state formation and query-time influence. We introduce PLACE, a factorized governance layer that adds write-side state certification and read-side authorization to a memory backend. A factorial evaluation on Mem0 with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B isolates the contribution of each mechanism. Results show that write-side governance substantially improves lifecycle state correctness, while read-side governance eliminates measured causal leakage from ineligible memory in the state-correct setting. Their combination achieves the strongest joint performance while preserving query-relevant support. These findings show that reliable persistent memory requires explicit control over both maintained state and query-time information influence.

title: An Information-Geometric Framework for OCS-Reconfigurable Interconnect Topology in Large-Scale AI Clusters
abstract: Optical Circuit Switches (OCS) make inter-pod wiring in AI clusters programmable, posing design questions on wiring choice, symmetry departure, and reconfigurations. We present a unified information-geometric framework to address these issues.A wiring is a point in a probability simplex over circuits within a degree polytope. Departure from a symmetric Fat-Tree prior $\mathbf{q}$ is measured by $\DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$. The cost $U$ is the smoothed DAG critical-path length, whose gradient equals path marginals of a Gibbs distribution via forward--backward recursion.For free energy $F_{β_1} = U + β_1^{-1} \DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$, we prove well-posedness, monotonic dependence on $β_1$, adaptation bounds via Jeffreys divergence, and a symmetry principle for static optimality. An entropic proximal-gradient method updates multiplicatively with a $|V|$-dim dual KL projection, achieving linear convergence.For time-varying traffic, a threshold policy yields regret $O(\sqrt{ΓC V_1 T})$ against the switching-free optimum. Traffic changes are detected by a multinomial GLR--CUSUM detector with non-asymptotic false-alarm bounds. Multi-job generalized-mean fairness aligns with $α$-fairness ($α\ge 2$). Experiments on pipeline, data, and MoE workloads validate the framework against integer programming.

title: World Models, Trees and Foundation Models for Retail Forecasting: Evidence from Four Public Data Sets
abstract: A retailer makes different decisions at different grains of the product, store and time hierarchy: store orders for an item in a store, supplier funding for an item across stores, category performance by store, and the financial plan for the chain. Which forecasting model to use depends on the grain. This paper compares models at each grain on four public data sets (M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat, and Corporación Favorita, the last kept out of all development), over rolling forecast origins with paired tests and model confidence sets. It covers price and promotion through the plan inputs these data record, not product, assortment or place. The models are a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, the same network without that state, LightGBM, the Temporal Fusion Transformer, TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral, seasonal naive, and an equal-weight average of the world model, LightGBM and TimesFM given the plan. The answer changed with the grain. For an item by store and an item across stores, the average had the lowest error on seven and eight of nine data sets, and the 90% confidence set held a median of 1 and 2 models. For a category by store, a category and the chain total, the lowest-error model differed between data sets and a median of 4 of nine models were not separated by the four to six windows available. For category-by-store planning cost, the average or LightGBM was lowest on seven of eight data sets, and the world model was lowest only on M5; it was behind LightGBM item by store on six of eight. Every trained model used the plan, and on the weekly promotion-driven data pretrained models were less accurate without it. These results hold for these data sets; a forecast solved across all four Ps, or a retailer's own data, may give different results. Every model, test and change that lost is reported.

title: M-JEPA: Predictive Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs with Scaffold-Shift Evaluation on Tox21
abstract: Self-supervised molecular representation learning is increasingly used to improve transfer on small, label-limited property prediction tasks, yet commonly used contrastive objectives can be sensitive to view construction and are often evaluated with protocols that report only discrimination. We adapt Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) to molecular graphs by masking chemically coherent connected subgraphs and training a context encoder to regress the masked target embedding produced by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher. To evaluate predictive self-supervision under realistic distribution shift, we introduce a leakage-resistant, compute-matched three-phase protocol: (i) an 80-run objective screening on ESOL with fixed compute budgets, (ii) JEPA-only refinement of masking and augmentation choices, and (iii) per-assay Tox21 evaluation under Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits with joint discrimination-reliability analysis and attribution diagnostics. Under matched compute, M-JEPA achieves substantially lower ESOL proxy RMSE than a compute-matched InfoNCE baseline (mean RMSE 2.12 vs 3.75; mean paired dRMSE 1.61; 95% bootstrap CI [1.52, 1.72]; Wilcoxon p=2.4e-4) and typically completes runs faster (~15-25 min vs ~35-45 min on a single GPU under identical hardware), albeit with higher runtime variance. On Tox21, improvements in ROC-AUC/PR-AUC are assay-dependent and do not uniformly imply better calibration; reliability diagrams and Brier/ECE metrics reveal endpoints where fine-tuning improves ranking but leaves probabilities miscalibrated.

title: Indistinguishable Agents: Training Agent Privacy as Twin-World Indistinguishability
abstract: LLM agents search, shop and send messages for their users, and every action is seen by some party. Existing privacy training rewards agents for not mentioning protected items, yet an observer can infer a private fact from what the agent does. Since an observer learns a fact only if its view changes with the fact, we propose \methodfull (\method), which trains on twin worlds that differ only in the private fact. A frozen distinguisher scores each observer's view by its log-likelihood ratio for the true world, and paired GRPO trains the agent on task success minus this ratio. We prove that this objective controls the Bayes success of every observer on every channel. On shopping and messaging tasks \method removes the leakage that disclosure judges and query-level rewards miss, while the agent still completes its tasks.

title: Legal Guidance in the Wild: How Users Seek Legal Help in Real-World LLM Conversations
abstract: People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute a multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how a request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations; and create a human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports a two-stage comparison of ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large against a TF-IDF cascade. Our framework supports large-scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development.
